newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt easily wins first vote on Albania force.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt easily wins first vote on Albania force.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Tuesday comfortably won a first vote in parliament on an Italian-led security force for Albania that has caused political turmoil, but his fragile alliance is not yet out of danger.

The centre-left government won a vote on its own resolution in the Senate (upper house) by 154 votes to 119 with two abstentions. The opposition centre-right Freedom Alliance voted against, resisting an appeal by Prodi for all-party support.
Its rival motion, which centre-right leader Silvio Berlusconi had wanted the government to back instead, was rejected after the government abstained.
Prodi's victory had been expected because he has a majority in the Senate but a bigger test awaits him on Wednesday when the lower Chamber of Deputies holds its vote.

The government cannot survive without support from the Communist Refoundation party in the Chamber. The hard-left party has refused to back the 6,000-strong force, due to deploy next week with a mandate to assist relief efforts in lawless Albania.
Refoundation's stance has caused a severe split in Prodi's alliance, which may have no choice but to vote for the opposition motion on Wednesday to ensure approval for the force.
Parliamentary party leaders from the ruling coalition in the Chamber were due to meet later on Tuesday to discuss the vote. Debate in the Chamber is due to begin at midday (1000 GMT).
Fabio Mussi, leftist leader in the lower house, said there was still time to work out a consensus motion with the Freedom Alliance. "There's no need for despair," he said.

Prodi told the Senate earlier that both Italian credibility abroad and the fate of Albanians would be at risk if Italy failed to live up to its task. The multinational force is the first of its kind to be led by Italy.

"The government is asking the whole parliament to support the effort that this country is being asked to make," Prodi said. "It is not rhetoric but the pure and simple truth to say that the whole world is watching us."

The Berlusconi bloc had initially signalled that it would back the government on sending the force, authorised by a U.N. Security Council resolution on March 28 after armed anarchy exploded in Albania, Europe's poorest state.

It abruptly switched stance on Tuesday after a deputy foreign minister, Piero Fassino, told a meeting of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) that the government believed Albania's rightist President Sali Berisha should leave office.
"Things like this expose our boys (soldiers) to greater risks" in Albania, Berlusconi said.

Fassino's remarks drew a strong protest from the Albanian Foreign Ministry. Prodi distanced himself from the comments and later wrote to Berisha and Prime Minister Bashkim Fino assuring them Italy would not meddle in internal Albanian affairs.

Rebel committees holding southern Albanian towns are demanding Berisha's immediate resignation, blaming him for failure to control popular but fraudulent savings schemes whose collapse sparked last month's explosion of violence.
He has said he will quit if his Democratic Party loses early elections due to take place by the end of June.
Prodi told the Senate that Italy expected the security force to stay in Albania for no more than six months and leave at the latest within one month of the elections.
Italy plans to send 2,500 troops, France some 1,000, Greece 700, Turkey 500, Romania 400 and Spain 300. Austria and Denmark say they are also considering participation.
